s0.p1: Everything connected to the Internet has an **_IP_** address, which uniquely identifies the Internet-connected device
s0.p2: There are two types of **_IP_** addresses: _public_ and _private_
s0.p3: Public addresses are accessible to everyone on the Internet
s0.p4: Private addresses are only accessible within a _local network_
s0.p5: For example, ⟦f0⟧ is a private IP address
s0.p6: It will never be a public IP address,
s0.p7: and there are millions of IP addresses like ⟦f1⟧ in the world
s0.p8: A device called a **router** is responsible for exchanging data packets between the local network and the public Internet
s0.p9: The router has a function which, for every Internet message (packet), creates a local IP address that uniquely corresponds to a public IP address, and vice versa (for returning packets)
s0.p10: Most public IP addresses have names known as DNS hostnames,
s0.p11: and so do many local IP addresses
s0.p12: For example, ⟦f2⟧ is a DNS hostname that has an IP address
s0.p13: If you type [echo command](⟦f3⟧) in the command-line interpreter
s0.p14: you can see that the computer has translated this hostname into an IP address, for example ⟦f4⟧, and is sending packets to it
s0.p15: Any device connected to the Internet has the universal hostname **_localhost_**,
s0.p16: and the universal IP address for **_localhost_** is the private IP address **⟦f5⟧**
s0.p17: This address is not recognised by the router
s0.p19: The optional prefix **_www_** in a website’s hostname implies that the internet device or host is responsible for serving an application on the **World Wide Web**
s0.p20: There are many types of applications that run on the Internet, not just on the World Wide Web, including, for example, email and FTP (File Transfer Protocol)
s1.p1: Data packets arriving at a device from the Internet almost always have a **port** allocated to them
s1.p2: This is a number in the range from 0 to 64k (65536)
s1.p3: ^^with the exception of certain reserved numbers and ranges^^
s1.p4: The World Wide Web uses port **80**
s1.p5: Email sent via the SMTP protocol uses port 25 (or 465 and 587)
s1.p6: **Ports** are simply identifiers on packets that indicate which application the data packets are intended for
s1.p7: Network software will listen on this port
s1.p8: When developers deploy a web application, they usually bind it to an alternative port rather than port 80
s1.p9: Port **8080** is often used for this purpose
s1.p10: ^^The number could be almost any port, for example, 2018 or 12345^^
s1.p11: ^^But 8080 is convenient because it is different from port 80, yet it is very similar to 80^^
s1.p12: ![ico-20 warn] Only one application can listen on a specific port on a given device
s1.p17: or (if it is connected to a network)
s1.p19: The **HTTP** (HyperText Transfer Protocol) used by the World Wide Web requires the hostname to be included in the request as a header or passed directly to the application
s1.p20: ^^So, **_http://127.0.0.1:8080/_**, where **localhost** is replaced by the IP address **127.0.0.1**, will reach the target application, but may not work correctly if the network application expects a request to **localhost**^^
s1.p21: The _Internet_ is a network infrastructure connecting millions of computers within the _Internet_ network
s1.p22: Any two computers connected to the Internet can communicate with one another
s1.p23: The _World Wide Web_ is a way of accessing information via the _Internet_
s1.p24: The World Wide Web uses the **HTTP** protocol to transfer data
